whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Sales Foundations exam for?

personas.label: New sales reps using Salesforce
personas.description: You work deals in Salesforce every day and want a credential that shows you know the tool.

personas.label: Sales managers
personas.description: You run a team on Salesforce and want to understand the pipeline and forecast properly.

personas.label: People moving into sales operations
personas.description: You support a sales team and need a grounding in how the process fits together.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Sales Foundations Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This is an entry-level exam. It mixes Salesforce basics with everyday selling: how a deal moves from lead to closed, what the pipeline shows, and which tool helps at each step. There is nothing to configure and no code.
bullets: 62% to pass, about 25 correct answers out of 40. Confirm it in the official exam guide before you book.
Process plus platform. Expect both selling concepts and the Salesforce feature that supports them.
Pipeline and forecasting come up often, so know what each stage and forecast category means.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You are ready when you can take a deal from lead to closed in Salesforce without help, and explain what the pipeline report is telling you. Aim for 80% or more on practice tests.

examFormat.heading: Sales Foundations Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Many questions describe something a rep needs to do, such as logging a call or chasing a stalled deal, and ask which Salesforce feature to use.
bestWayToPass: Follow one deal end to end: Lead, qualification, conversion, opportunity, products, close. Know what each record is for.
Learn the pipeline vocabulary: Stage, probability, close date, amount and forecast category.
Know the productivity tools: Tasks and events, email logging, mobile and the Kanban view.
Read a report: Understand what a pipeline report and a simple dashboard are telling you.

certificationCard.description: An entry-level exam covering the day-to-day of selling in Salesforce: leads and opportunities, the pipeline, forecasting, activity tracking, and the reports that show how the team is doing.

keyConcepts.h2: Sales Foundations: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Leads, Accounts, Contacts and Opportunities
blocks.body: A **Lead** is someone who might become a customer but has not been qualified yet. When they look real, you **convert** the lead, which creates an **Account** (the company), a **Contact** (the person) and usually an **Opportunity** (the potential deal). Converting is one-way, so do it when the lead is genuinely qualified. An Account can have many Contacts and many Opportunities over time, which is how repeat business is tracked. Knowing which record holds which information is the foundation of everything else in this exam.

blocks.heading: The Pipeline: Stages, Amount and Close Date
blocks.body: An **Opportunity** carries a **stage** showing how far along it is, an **amount**, and a **close date**. Each stage has a **probability**, and the pipeline is the collection of open opportunities across stages. A **forecast category** groups stages into buckets such as Pipeline, Best Case, Commit and Closed, which is how managers judge what will land this quarter. Keeping the close date honest matters more than it looks: a pipeline full of overdue close dates tells a manager nothing. Reps move deals through stages as real progress happens, not to look busy.

blocks.heading: Working the Deal: Activities and Productivity
blocks.body: **Tasks** are things to do and **events** are meetings in the calendar, and both can be linked to a lead, contact, account or opportunity so the history stays with the record. Emails can be logged automatically so conversations are visible to the team. The **Kanban** view lets reps drag opportunities between stages. **Path** shows the guidance and required fields for the current stage. The Salesforce **mobile app** covers the same work away from a desk. **Chatter** lets a rep ask a question on the record itself, so the answer is kept with the deal rather than lost in email.

blocks.heading: Products, Quotes and Teams
blocks.body: An opportunity can have **products** added from a **price book**, which sets what was sold and at what price, and that is where the amount usually comes from. A **quote** can be generated from those products and sent to the customer. When several people work one deal, an **opportunity team** records who is involved and what their role is. Larger deals may need an **approval** before a discount is given. None of this needs configuration knowledge for this exam: you need to recognise what each feature is for.

blocks.heading: Reports, Dashboards and Forecasts
blocks.body: A **report** lists or summarises records, such as all open opportunities closing this quarter. A **dashboard** shows several reports as charts on one screen, which is how managers see the team at a glance. **Forecasting** rolls opportunity amounts up through the team so a manager can see what is expected to close, using the forecast categories. **List views** give a quick filtered list on a tab, which most reps use daily. For the exam, know which of these answers a given question: a single filtered list, a summary, a visual overview, or a projection of what will close.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Sales Foundations Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions describe a rep's day and ask which feature fits. Match the task to the record or tool built for it.

blocks.heading: Leads and Conversion
blocks.body: Leads are unqualified. Converting creates an Account, a Contact and usually an Opportunity, and cannot be undone.

blocks.heading: Opportunity Management
blocks.body: Stage, amount and close date drive the pipeline. Forecast categories group stages into what managers commit to.

blocks.heading: Activity Management
blocks.body: Tasks for to-dos, events for meetings, both linked to the record so the history stays in one place.

blocks.heading: Reports and Dashboards
blocks.body: Reports list and summarise, dashboards visualise several reports, list views give a quick filtered list.

blocks.heading: Teams and Quotes
blocks.body: Opportunity teams record who is working a deal. Products and price books set what is being sold, and quotes go to the customer.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: Good next steps after Sales Foundations:

sampleQuestions.question: A rep has a business card from a conference for someone who has shown mild interest but has not been qualified. Which record should they create?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Leads hold people who might become customers but have not been qualified yet.
whyWrong: An Opportunity is a specific potential deal, which does not exist yet.
Accounts represent companies you already do business with or are actively working.
A Quote is a priced proposal, which is much further along.

sampleQuestions.question: A lead has been qualified and there is a real deal to pursue. What does converting the lead create?
options: A Quote and then a signed Contract
sampleQuestions.explanation: Conversion turns the lead into the company, the person and the potential deal.
whyWrong: Quotes and contracts come later, after there is an opportunity.
The contact and the opportunity are created as well.
Cases are for service issues, not sales.

sampleQuestions.question: Which three fields most directly define where a deal sits in the pipeline?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Stage shows progress, amount shows value, and close date shows when it is expected to land.
whyWrong: Those describe where the lead came from and what the company is like.
Those are company details, not deal progress.
Those belong to Cases in service, not opportunities.

sampleQuestions.question: A manager wants to know what is likely to close this quarter, not just everything that is open. Which feature gives that?
options: A list view of all accounts
sampleQuestions.explanation: Forecasting rolls opportunity amounts up by category, separating what is committed from what is merely in the pipeline.
whyWrong: The activity timeline shows what has happened on a record.
A list of accounts says nothing about expected revenue.
Lead queues hold unworked leads.

sampleQuestions.question: A rep needs to record a phone call they just made to a contact, so the history stays with the record. What should they use?
options: Log an activity against the contact
Write it down in a personal notebook
sampleQuestions.explanation: Activities such as logged calls and tasks attach to the record, so anyone looking at it later sees the history.
whyWrong: The person is already a contact, so a new lead would duplicate them.
A private note is invisible to the team.
Stage reflects deal progress, not a phone call.

sampleQuestions.question: Which view lets a rep drag opportunities from one stage to the next?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Kanban shows opportunities as cards by stage, and reps can drag them as deals progress.
whyWrong: Reports list and summarise but are not used to move deals.
Setup is for administrators.
Dashboards display charts, they do not update records.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the relationship between an Account and a Contact?
options: They are two words for the same record
Accounts are only used in service and Contacts only in sales
An Account is the company and Contacts are the people at it
sampleQuestions.explanation: The company is the Account and the people who work there are its Contacts.
whyWrong: They hold different information and serve different purposes.
Both are used across sales and service.
It is the other way round: an account has many contacts.

sampleQuestions.question: A rep wants to add what is being sold, with prices, to a deal. What should they use?
options: A brand new lead created for each product
Products from a price book on the opportunity
sampleQuestions.explanation: Products come from a price book and are added to the opportunity, which usually sets the amount.
whyWrong: Chatter is for conversation.
Tasks are to-dos, not line items.
Leads are unqualified people, not products.

sampleQuestions.question: Three colleagues are working the same large deal and the business wants that recorded. What fits?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Opportunity teams record everyone involved in a deal and what their role is.
whyWrong: Cases are for customer issues.
Three opportunities would triple the forecast for one deal.
A lead can only be converted once.

sampleQuestions.question: A manager wants one screen showing pipeline by stage, deals closing this month and team performance. What should be built?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dashboards place several reports as charts on one screen for an at-a-glance view.
whyWrong: Quotes are proposals for customers.
A list view shows one filtered list of records.
Price books hold product prices.

sampleQuestions.question: Why does an accurate close date matter?
options: It creates a support case automatically each time
Forecasts and pipeline reports depend on it
sampleQuestions.explanation: Close dates drive the time-based view of the pipeline, so wrong dates make forecasts meaningless.
whyWrong: Ownership is set separately.
Prices come from the price book.
Cases are created in service processes.

sampleQuestions.question: A rep asks a product question and wants the answer kept with the deal for others to see. What fits best?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Chatter keeps the conversation attached to the record, so the next person sees it.
whyWrong: A task is a to-do, not a discussion.
Renaming the account loses data and answers nothing.
Email is invisible to colleagues unless logged.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a forecast category do?
options: Groups stages into buckets such as Commit
Decides which user ends up owning the account
sampleQuestions.explanation: Forecast categories group stages so managers can separate confident revenue from early pipeline.
whyWrong: Access is controlled by the administrator.
Ownership is a separate field.
Prices come from price books.

sampleQuestions.question: A rep needs their deals and contacts while visiting a customer, away from their laptop. What should they use?
options: Nothing is available off a desktop
A printed report from last month
sampleQuestions.explanation: The mobile app gives access to the same records and lets the rep log activity on the spot.
whyWrong: Salesforce is available on mobile.
A spreadsheet is not shared and quickly drifts from the real data.
A printout goes out of date and cannot be updated.

sampleQuestions.question: Which is the best description of a pipeline report?
options: A record of all of the past invoices
sampleQuestions.explanation: The pipeline is the set of open deals, and a pipeline report groups them so you can see where they sit.
whyWrong: Employee records are not the sales pipeline.
Invoices are billing records, usually in another system.
Cases belong to service.
